public_rationale: The claim has two parts: (a) LLMs were writing more code, and (b) the security and trustworthiness of that code had not been established by the post on 11 February 2026. The test period runs from 1 October 2024 to 11 February 2026. On (a), a peer-reviewed study in Science, publicized on 22 January 2026, found that AI-assisted coding in the US rose from about 5% in 2022 to nearly 30% in the last quarter of 2024. The data came from Python contributions on GitHub (e1). On (b), Veracode reported on 30 July 2025 that LLMs introduced vulnerabilities in 45% of its test cases. It said models were getting better at coding accurately but not at security (e2). A preprint posted on 2 December 2025 found that 61% of solutions from SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet were functionally correct, but only 10.5% were secure (e3). The packet has no evidence from before the post showing that AI-generated code was reliably secure. Both parts meet the support condition.
limitations: The code-share data cover open-source Python on GitHub through early 2025. They do not cover all code or the months just before the post.
The security evidence comes from benchmark tasks in a vendor report and a preprint, not from audits of deployed code.
Correctness is measured only on the preprint's benchmark tasks and mentioned in general terms by Veracode. Maintainability and other aspects of trustworthiness are not measured.

criteria.support_condition: Data show the share of code written with AI rising, and credible studies show AI-generated code frequently has security flaws, so its trustworthiness is not established.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Data show AI coding is not growing, or credible evidence before the post shows AI-generated code is reliably secure and trustworthy.
